Rhino IVF

By: Laura Byrne | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Cutting edge science to save a species on the brink of extinction

Unique Selling Point:
The team that brought us Africa's first cloned animal in 2003 is bringing cutting edge fertility science to bear on the problem of wildlife populations under threat. Dr Morne de la Rey of Embryo Plus was also the first to bring an IVF buffalo into the world in 2016. Since 2017 he has been focusing his efforts on rhino, which do not breed successfully in captivity and are under lethal pressure in the wild. Using hormone stimulation, artificial insemination and even IVF, Dr de la Rey is hoping to help captive species of rhino breed at a rate that can combat the losses in the wild. He has already had considerable success.

Summary:
Experience and research show rhinos in captivity often develop menopause or premature reproductive problems; and siblings or groups of similar age don't stimulate each other. This means rescued orphan rhinos don't naturally reproduce. At Thaba Manzi, there is a group of 5 orphans that failed to conceive for 3 years. Enter Dr de la Rey. He's performed procedures on these rhinos including hormone stimulation, removal of cysts and follicles - and helped all of them conceive. Today, some of their babies are falling pregnant, showing promise for population growth.

This is just the beginning. Last year, De la Rey's team performed the world's first progesterone synchronised artificial insemination. On farms, rhino can be regularly herded up and scanned to check where in their natural cycle they are, then injected with semen. But in the wild, this is more difficult and it’s desirable to be able to fertilize all the females at the same time. So they insert a progesterone device to bring the females onto their cycle. They can then be injected with the semen at a time when pregnancy will be likely. This allows genetic variation to be injected into a wild population without the stress, risk and cost of bringing a bull into a population with no guarantee of success. De la Rey can also scan for pregnancy, telling the foetus's age more accurately than lab progesterone tests. This is essential because pregnant females are transported to help repopulate reserves, but if pregnancy is too advanced they abort or give birth prematurely. With this method, transport is cheaper, kinder and more successful.

The next step is IVF. De la Rey estimates he will have the first southern white rhino IVF babies by November this year.

Further information:
The glamorous goal in all this is to rescue the Northern White Rhino from extinction: there are only two left in the world (both females) and neither of them is able to breed. In the 1970s when the wild population was fading but still fairly large, 40 northern white rhino were captured and taken to various zoos around the world. After the last wild one was spotted in the 1990s, this population became the hope for survival of the species. It was always hoped that they would naturally breed, but this didn’t happen. In around 2009, there were only 8 left. Four were sent to Kenya and the last four died in zoos. Over the next few years, it was hoped that they would breed in the wild, but they didn’t and one of the males died abruptly. In around 2011, the owner, Dvurkralove Zoo signed an exclusive deal with IZW Berlin. The last male, Sudan, then died in 2018, but some of his sperm was frozen – by Morne, who claims that IZW then stole it from his lab in Kenya, which is on the Dvurkralove property. Since then, IZW has harvested eggs from the females and made embryos. They haven’t perfected the implant technique yet, so they have frozen the embryos. Morne says he wants to perfect the whole process on southern white rhino before he risks it on the northern white rhino. He says he knows the implant process will work across the subspecies because it worked on 2 subspecies of sable which have the same degree of difference. He also says his focus is any conservation species - this science is relevant across the field, not only for rhino.

The main limiting factor in perfecting the process is money, he says: they only cycle about 10 eggs/month at the moment which means it’s difficult to get the repeats he needs to get the process right. There are two different methods: free-swimming fertilization, which doesn’t work very well. They only got embryos of 4 cells which did not survive. They then recently got an ICSI machine: intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection. This injects the sperm directly into the egg. They have since attempted a few but no luck so far. He says the medium in which the mebryos are grown is the challenging factor.

What can we show?
At his lab in Brits, we can show injection of an egg with sperm (possibly a cow egg but he says you won’t be able to tell).
In the field, we can spend a day in the Warmbaths area with them. we’ll collect semen from bull rhino and then watch it being injected into cows.We can also watch collection of eggs from the cows, which will then be used for IVF.
Lab work – sperm injections. Culture of embryos. That’s fast, 30 secs of a minute of material. Other option is to go out with them and do photography of the work, scanning, aspiration, etc. takes an hour. Collecting ovocytes. One of the places is in Bela Bela, also Maritaba (Marikele), Barberton, Swartkloof. Several sites. Can arrange a visit at Swartkloof.
We can also see the rhinos which were infertile and now have calves which are reproducing themselves. It’s a message about maintaining a population in captivity. Some organisations don’t approve and say we should rather put money towards conserving them in the wild – we can try to find a voice to say this.

11 March 2020: CAR HIRE for travel to Zwartkloof Game Reserve AND Thaba Manzi Wildlife Services (both Bela Bela area) and back to Joburg - WITH PRESENTER AND FULL CREW

Script:


VO1: The rhino: it’s one of Africa’s most iconic species. But with populations decimated by poaching, many now survive in hidden locations, behind high electrified fences.
UPSOUND: Hendrik Hansen: The two rhinos, they were both born on the farm here and then there was a very bad poaching incident where five rhinos was poached.
VO2: Tia and Fia were hand-reared after they were both orphaned a few years ago, says wildlife vet Dr Hendrik Hansen.
UPSOUND: Hendrik Hansen: The whole other herd were moved to a safe area. And to introduce these two animals into that area, the social structure of these animals is always going to make it difficult.
VO3: Two isolated females, with no potential mate: it’s a reproductive dead end…especially because rhino do not breed easily in captivity, where close proximity means stress levels are high.
UPSOUND: Hendrik Hansen: In a lot of situations where you’ve got orphaned rhinos, you don’t get that the animals of the same age would actually breed because there’s not a normal social structure in the herd.
VO4: But today, Hansen is part of a team working to create a future for orphans like these.
UPSOUND: Morne de la Rey: Today you will see how easy it is or how easy it looks. But it took us nearly a year to find the ovaries.
VO5: Dr Morné de la Rey has a long family history with assisted reproduction in domestic animals. In 2003, his team made history with Futhi, the first animal cloned in Africa. After mastering in vitro fertilisation in cattle, and world firsts producing in vitro buffalo, sable and wildebeest, De la Rey set his sights on rhino.
LINK: Morne and his team are busy preparing to perform a high tech procedure on two young female rhinos.
VO6: They will collect oocytes – egg cells – from Tia and Fia.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: How many eggs are we hoping to collect today?
Morne de la Rey: If we collect one egg out of a rhino, I’m extremely extremely happy.
UPSOUND: Morne de la Rey: We must understand that that rhino is huge. It's two tons big. It's 4m long, it’s a metre and a half wide. The ovaries we eventually found it about a metre, a metre and a half inside the rhino. The ovary is 4cm, 5cm big. Inside the ovary is a follicle which is 4mm big. Inside the follicle is the egg which is 40 microns big.
LINK: This is Tia and she’s currently under anaesthetic. And her vitals will be monitored very very closely while the team harvests oocytes from this two-tonne adolescent rhino. The entire procedure will take about an hour and a half.
VO7: The first step is to clear the rectum of dung...
UPSOUND: Claire: It’s so nice and warm!
VO: ...and I get intimately involved.
Wow guys. Rhino dung. Eau de rhino dung.
VO8: Next, de la Rey inserts a probe of his own design, and uses ultrasound to locate the ovaries.
UPSOUND: Morne de la Rey: Ok, there’s the ovary. The black spots that you see there, those are the follicles.
VO9: A fine needle flushes fluid into the follicles and washes out the microscopic eggs.
UPSOUND: Morne de la Rey: You see how it collapses and it re-expands? That’s now perfect.
VO10: It’s an almost unthinkably delicate process.
UPSOUND: Morne de la Rey: If you are three kilometers in the sky. And somewhere on a field that is 16 rugby fields long eight rugby fields wide and a golf ball is somewhere on there and you got to shoot with a bow and arrow an arrow into that golf ball. From three kilometres in the sky. It’s exactly the same.
VO11: The team collects a total of six eggs, which are taken to the laboratory and injected with sperm, using the same technology as human IVF.
LINK: It’s hard to believe that this high-tech environment has much to do with the wild animals we’ve just seen. But taking sophisticated science into natural habitats might give this species a chance of survival.
VO12: Nowhere is this more urgent than in the case of the northern white rhino, featured in David Attenborough’s latest series, Seven Worlds One Planet. The last bull died in 2018; only two females, Najin and Fatu, survive.
UPSOUND: David Attenborough: These two females are the last of their kind. When they die, an entire subspecies that inhabited the earth for millions of years will have disappeared forever.
VO13: Last year, a European group of scientists harvested eggs from Najin and Fatu and fertilised them with sperm taken from two males before their deaths. Three embryos were created and frozen, waiting for transfer to a southern white rhino surrogate.
But the technology is still in its infancy.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: How many successful babies have we had through IVF in rhino?
Morne de la Rey: Not a single animal has been born from IVF anywhere in the world.
VO14: Nevertheless, De la Rey has made significant progress, developing Africa’s first rhino morula embryo, one step away from being mature enough to implant.
UPSOUND: Morne de la Rey: The problem that we're facing is that every species is different. They are differently built, their size are different. They are also hormonally different. So everything we've got to discover from the word go.
VO15: Meanwhile, he’s pioneering another breakthrough. Breeding Tia and Fia the traditional way would mean importing a bull from another farm – a risky, costly procedure with no guarantee of success. Artificial insemination could streamline the process.
LINK: Two weeks ago we collected oocytes from Tia and Fia and they were fitted with devices to stimulate hormone production. Today, the process comes full circle as we’re collecting semen from Finn that will be used to artificially inseminate the females in the hopes of beginning a new generation.
VO16: Finn is one of several rhinos at Thaba Manzi. Many of them have been moved here from larger farms and parks to keep them safe from poachers.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: So right now, you are actually manually stimulating him?
Morne de la Rey: Yes. And by stimulating it here at the back you then stimulate those glands to do the ejaculation.
VO17: Within hours, Finn’s semen has been delivered to Tia and Fia, who, thanks to the progesterone-releasing devices inserted two weeks ago, should be on heat and ready to receive it.
UPSOUND: Hendrik Hansen: Our belief is definitely that once they are pregnant and once they have got a calf at foot and once there are different age animals in the group, they will probably be able to carry on breeding naturally.
LINK: Today we saw two rhinos that were rescued from the clutches of poachers. It looks like a lonely fate but it is in these two that lies the hope for generations to come.
VO18: De la Rey will soon know whether the artificial insemination has been successful. And as for IVF, he says it’s only a matter of time.
UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: I love going to baby showers and I really want to go to a baby shower for Tia and Fia. So do you anticipate a success with them? And when would that be? Just so I can buy a gift - it's a boy, it's a girl.
Morne de la Rey: You can start buying gifts okay. We 100 percent will be successful. We will be at the end of the day have a rhino test tube baby or in vitro baby. We will not stop before we are successful.

PROMOS
1. The rhino: it’s one of our most most threatened species. But the team that brought us Africa’s first cloned animal is perfecting in vitro fertilisation: a radical solution to boost waning populations.

2. You’ve heard of a test tube baby, but what about a test tube rhino? We meet the scientists working to develop in vitro fertilisation for one of Africa’s most iconic species.

3. Rhino populations are under pressure from poaching, and orphans in captivity often fail to breed naturally. New technology is offering a future for these animals and generations to come.

Breeding Tia and Fia the traditional way would mean importing a bull from another farm – a risky, costly procedure with no guarantee of success. Artificial insemination could streamline the process. LINK: Two weeks ago we collected oocytes from Tia and Fia and they were fitted with devices to stimulate hormone production. Today, the process comes full circle as we’re collecting semen from Finn that will be used to artificially inseminate the females in the hopes of beginning a new generation. VO16: Finn is one of several rhinos at Thaba Manzi. Many of them have been moved here from larger farms and parks to keep them safe from poachers. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: So right now, you are actually manually stimulating him? Morne de la Rey: Yes. And by stimulating it here at the back you then stimulate those glands to do the ejaculation. VO17: Within hours, Finn’s semen has been delivered to Tia and Fia, who, thanks to the progesterone-releasing devices inserted two weeks ago, should be on heat and ready to receive it. UPSOUND: Hendrik Hansen: Our belief is definitely that once they are pregnant and once they have got a calf at foot and once there are different age animals in the group, they will probably be able to carry on breeding naturally. LINK: Today we saw two rhinos that were rescued from the clutches of poachers. It looks like a lonely fate but it is in these two that lies the hope for generations to come. VO18: De la Rey will soon know whether the artificial insemination has been successful. And as for IVF, he says it’s only a matter of time. UPSOUND: Claire Mawisa: I love going to baby showers and I really want to go to a baby shower for Tia and Fia. So do you anticipate a success with them? And when would that be? Just so I can buy a gift - it's a boy, it's a girl. Morne de la Rey: You can start buying gifts okay. We 100 percent will be successful. We will be at the end of the day have a rhino test tube baby or in vitro baby. We will not stop before we are successful. PROMOS 1. The rhino: it’s one of our most most threatened species. But the team that brought us Africa’s first cloned animal is perfecting in vitro fertilisation: a radical solution to boost waning populations. 2. You’ve heard of a test tube baby, but what about a test tube rhino? We meet the scientists working to develop in vitro fertilisation for one of Africa’s most iconic species. 3. Rhino populations are under pressure from poaching, and orphans in captivity often fail to breed naturally. New technology is offering a future for these animals and generations to come.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Cutting edge science to save a species on the brink of extinction
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The team that brought us Africa's first cloned animal in 2003 is bringing cutting edge fertility science to bear on the problem of wildlife populations under threat. Dr Morne de la Rey of Embryo Plus was also the first to bring an IVF buffalo into the world in 2016. Since 2017 he has been focusing his efforts on rhino, which do not breed successfully in captivity and are under lethal pressure in the wild. Using hormone stimulation, artificial insemination and even IVF, Dr de la Rey is hoping to help captive species of rhino breed at a rate that can combat the losses in the wild. He has already had considerable success.
metadata.Summary: Experience and research show rhinos in captivity often develop menopause or premature reproductive problems; and siblings or groups of similar age don't stimulate each other. This means rescued orphan rhinos don't naturally reproduce. At Thaba Manzi, there is a group of 5 orphans that failed to conceive for 3 years. Enter Dr de la Rey. He's performed procedures on these rhinos including hormone stimulation, removal of cysts and follicles - and helped all of them conceive. Today, some of their babies are falling pregnant, showing promise for population growth. This is just the beginning. Last year, De la Rey's team performed the world's first progesterone synchronised artificial insemination. On farms, rhino can be regularly herded up and scanned to check where in their natural cycle they are, then injected with semen. But in the wild, this is more difficult and it’s desirable to be able to fertilize all the females at the same time. So they insert a progesterone device to bring the females onto their cycle. They can then be injected with the semen at a time when pregnancy will be likely. This allows genetic variation to be injected into a wild population without the stress, risk and cost of bringing a bull into a population with no guarantee of success. De la Rey can also scan for pregnancy, telling the foetus's age more accurately than lab progesterone tests. This is essential because pregnant females are transported to help repopulate reserves, but if pregnancy is too advanced they abort or give birth prematurely. With this method, transport is cheaper, kinder and more successful. The next step is IVF. De la Rey estimates he will have the first southern white rhino IVF babies by November this year.
metadata.Further information: The glamorous goal in all this is to rescue the Northern White Rhino from extinction: there are only two left in the world (both females) and neither of them is able to breed. In the 1970s when the wild population was fading but still fairly large, 40 northern white rhino were captured and taken to various zoos around the world. After the last wild one was spotted in the 1990s, this population became the hope for survival of the species. It was always hoped that they would naturally breed, but this didn’t happen. In around 2009, there were only 8 left. Four were sent to Kenya and the last four died in zoos. Over the next few years, it was hoped that they would breed in the wild, but they didn’t and one of the males died abruptly. In around 2011, the owner, Dvurkralove Zoo signed an exclusive deal with IZW Berlin. The last male, Sudan, then died in 2018, but some of his sperm was frozen – by Morne, who claims that IZW then stole it from his lab in Kenya, which is on the Dvurkralove property. Since then, IZW has harvested eggs from the females and made embryos. They haven’t perfected the implant technique yet, so they have frozen the embryos. Morne says he wants to perfect the whole process on southern white rhino before he risks it on the northern white rhino. He says he knows the implant process will work across the subspecies because it worked on 2 subspecies of sable which have the same degree of difference. He also says his focus is any conservation species - this science is relevant across the field, not only for rhino. The main limiting factor in perfecting the process is money, he says: they only cycle about 10 eggs/month at the moment which means it’s difficult to get the repeats he needs to get the process right. There are two different methods: free-swimming fertilization, which doesn’t work very well. They only got embryos of 4 cells which did not survive. They then recently got an ICSI machine: intra-cytoplasmic sperm injection. This injects the sperm directly into the egg. They have since attempted a few but no luck so far. He says the medium in which the mebryos are grown is the challenging factor. What can we show? At his lab in Brits, we can show injection of an egg with sperm (possibly a cow egg but he says you won’t be able to tell). In the field, we can spend a day in the Warmbaths area with them. we’ll collect semen from bull rhino and then watch it being injected into cows.We can also watch collection of eggs from the cows, which will then be used for IVF. Lab work – sperm injections. Culture of embryos. That’s fast, 30 secs of a minute of material. Other option is to go out with them and do photography of the work, scanning, aspiration, etc. takes an hour. Collecting ovocytes. One of the places is in Bela Bela, also Maritaba (Marikele), Barberton, Swartkloof. Several sites. Can arrange a visit at Swartkloof. We can also see the rhinos which were infertile and now have calves which are reproducing themselves. It’s a message about maintaining a population in captivity. Some organisations don’t approve and say we should rather put money towards conserving them in the wild – we can try to find a voice to say this.
